claims.text: Partially replacing Ti or Zr with additional Mo in a refractory high-entropy alloy will improve elevated-temperature mechanical strength.
HfMoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW are appropriate baseline compositions for the proposed Ti- or Zr-to-Mo substitution.
Increasing the Mo fraction while reducing a lower-melting-point element will increase the alloy's average melting point.
Increasing the Mo fraction will increase the alloy's shear modulus.
Mo has a high melting point.
Replacing Ti or Zr with Mo will increase lattice distortion and solid-solution strengthening.
The enhanced solid-solution strengthening will increase resistance to edge-dislocation motion.
Greater resistance to edge-dislocation motion will improve elevated-temperature strength.
The Mo-enriched alloy will have at least approximately 10% higher elevated-temperature yield strength than the baseline.
The predicted strength improvement will hold from approximately 800°C to 1600°C.
The proposed alloys are potentially relevant to high-temperature nuclear reactor structural applications.
The proposed alloys are potentially relevant to aerospace components.
The improvement requires retention of a single-phase solid solution without deleterious precipitation.
Prior work designed Hf0.5MoNbTaW and HfMoNbTaW by replacing Ti and Zr in HfMoNbTaTiZr with W to increase melting point and Young's modulus.
Prior work investigated solution strengthening and the contribution of edge-dislocation-induced strength in Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-W refractory alloys.
The magnitude of any strength increase may depend on substitution level and processing conditions, with unresolved ductility and phase-stability trade-offs.

contradictions.description: The example baselines HfMoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW already contain Mo but contain neither Ti nor Zr, so the stated intervention cannot reduce Ti or Zr in those baseline compositions.
The hypothesis proposes replacing Ti or Zr with Mo, whereas the cited same-family study replaced Ti and Zr with W; the evidence therefore does not directly instantiate the proposed intervention.
